variants.reconstruction:
%n ... | ib[rī? | ...]
#note: See @bib{RN117@322}: “Bottéro understood the first word as a 3rd fem. sing. stative, evidently @i{damqat} (‘[Ton rêve est de bo]n augure, [Mon am]i!’; cf. Tournay and Shaffer), but a close comparison between the signs @akk{LA} and @akk{AD} in this tablet shows that the first complete sign is the former, not the latter (the difference lies in the bottom wedge of the second row of horizontals, which in @akk{LA} falls further forward than the wedges immediately above it; see typically i 5', 9, iv 3').”
variants.intertext: The fragment’s obverse relates dreams from the Journey to the Cedar Forest; the reverse the story of Gilgameš, Ištar and the Bull of Heaven, and is much condensed and afflicted by errors of transmission when compared to later versions. To judge from the curvature of the inscribed surfaces, the fragment comes from near the bottom left-hand corner of a big, multi-columned tablet. At least forty lines are missing from the top edge, one or two only from the bottom.

variants.reconstruction:
%n irtakas | ana enkīdu | ... [...]
#note: See @bib{RN117@324}: “The word @i{irtakas} plausibly ends the narrative of Gilgameš’s toilet. As Bottéro rightly saw, Enkidu is not wanted here and his name is presumably an error. Bottéro exchanged it for Gilgameš, restoring the second divine determinative as @akk{{d}[iš₈-tar]}. Alternatively, one could assume that the text is much nearer to SB VI, which begins the narrative of Ištar’s advances with the line @i{ana dumqī ša Gilgāmeš īnī ittaši rubûtu Ištar}. In that case MB Boǧ₂’s @akk{a-na {d}en-ki-dum} would be another corruption under dictation, for @i{a-na dum-qí}, and the second divine determinative would introduce the name of Gilgameš.”
